alalal-c48460-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 22: whether an angel moves locally.

alalal-c48460-d1e113.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's mention of the great dispute about change of place.

alalal-c48460-d1e125.summary: Announces that the question of angelic motion will be divided into three parts to clarify its difficulties.

alalal-c48460-d1e135.summary: Lists the three parts: whether an angel moves locally, how it moves locally, and whether its motion is in time or in an instant.

alalal-c48460-d1e151.summary: First objection, from Physics VI: an indivisible moving through space must first traverse a space equal to itself, so it moves through indivisibles; since any space contains infinitely many and these cannot be traversed in finite time, an indivisible cannot move. An angel is indivisible, so it cannot move locally.

alalal-c48460-d1e203.summary: Second objection: what moves from A to B is partly in each terminus, and so is quantitatively divisible; an angel is not, so it is immobile.

alalal-c48460-d1e225.summary: Third objection: the Philosopher says motion of an indivisible is possible only if time were composed of nows, which it is not.

alalal-c48460-d1e243.summary: Fourth objection: a moving thing is in part of the space before the whole, so a slower mover would be in a smaller space; since every mobile occupies a space equal to itself, an indivisible space would be divided, which is impossible.

alalal-c48460-d1e272.summary: Rejects the common reply that Aristotle's arguments concern only indivisibles with position in the continuum, like points, and not angels: if so, the unit, which lacks position, could move, which philosophers deny even more strongly than of the point.

alalal-c48460-d1e317.summary: Adds that if position were the key, the philosophers would have argued from it, yet all their arguments rest on indivisibility itself.

alalal-c48460-d1e335.summary: Fifth objection: all motion arises from need; an angel, especially a blessed one, has no need, so it does not move.

alalal-c48460-d1e348.summary: Sixth objection: an act belongs naturally only to what has potency for it; an angel cannot have potency for natural rectilinear motion, being neither heavy nor light, nor for progressive motion, which requires organs like feet or wings.

alalal-c48460-d1e385.summary: Seventh objection: in whatever moves, mover and moved differ, and these are hard or impossible to find in an angel.

alalal-c48460-d1e401.summary: Eighth objection: whatever moves locally other than circularly also has potency to other changes, especially generation; an angel does not, so it cannot move rectilinearly, ascending or descending.

alalal-c48460-d1e421.summary: Ninth objection: no natural mover moves to contrary places, and voluntary movers move only to places that preserve their nature; so an angel would move only within the empyrean, its congenial place, and never come to earth.

alalal-c48460-d1e459.summary: Sed contra: the authority of the saints, especially Damascene, who says the angel by the swiftness of its nature passes quickly and works in diverse places; so it moves.

alalal-c48460-d1e481.summary: Further from Damascene: angels are found at once wherever the divine command directs, by the agility of their nature; other authorities could be added.

alalal-c48460-d1e494.summary: Argument by reason: what has power not multiplied through a medium and is not everywhere by essence can act only where it is; the angel is such a substance, defined in place, so it acts only where it is.

alalal-c48460-d1e518.summary: Continues: the inanimate medium between heaven and earth cannot receive the angel's intellectual power, so the angel acts only where it is; since it acts in different places successively (Damascene), it is in them successively, which is local motion.
claims: An angel's successive action in different places implies local motion.

alalal-c48460-d1e544.summary: Solution: angels move locally, as the saints say, whatever the philosophers may hold.

alalal-c48460-d1e555.summary: Reply to the first objections: an indivisible whose very being is indivisibility, like the point or unit, which are principles and termini of quantity, is immobile and has no place. The angel's indivisibility in quantity follows from its being and is not its essence, so it can move in virtue of being a spiritual substance whose power overcomes every obstacle, Damascene's 'swiftness of nature'. Its motion overcomes spatial distance, is not proportioned to or measured by time, and passes through any medium as through a void. Such motion is above nature, not against or below it.
claims: Aristotle's arguments apply to things whose essence is indivisibility, not to angels, whose indivisibility follows from their being.
Angelic motion overcomes spatial distance and is neither proportioned to nor measured by time; it is above nature.

alalal-c48460-d1e644.summary: On the common reply: Albert agrees that it fails, since it is certainly not what the Philosopher meant.

alalal-c48460-d1e655.summary: Reply on need: motion is not always from need; it may show power, as runners run, or show service, as a soldier gladly moves in the king's service without need on either side. Or it may be for our need, or to merit the glory they had before merit.
claims: Angelic motion may manifest power or service rather than satisfy need.

alalal-c48460-d1e688.summary: Reply on the Philosopher's dictum: he speaks of natural and progressive motion, not of supramundane motion.

alalal-c48460-d1e697.summary: Reply on potency: the angel received such a potency for motion in the creation of its nature.
claims: The angel's power to move was given with its nature at creation.

alalal-c48460-d1e706.summary: Further reply: the objection holds of natural and progressive motion, not of the motion of supramundane substances.

alalal-c48460-d1e722.summary: Reply on mover and moved: in the angel the will moves and the angel is moved, as soul moves body in an animal, or as form moves matter in rising fire, which is out of place only accidentally; the potency is given for need, though the act may be exercised without need.
claims: In the angel the will is mover and the angelic substance is moved.

alalal-c48460-d1e756.summary: Reply to the remaining objections: they apply where motion to form and to place coincide, as in heavy and light bodies, whose mover is the generator or what removes an obstacle, since the generator gives form and its accidents, chief among them local motion (Physics VIII). Angelic motion is not of this kind.
claims: Angelic motion is not natural motion following from generation.

alalal-c48460.summary: Article 22 opens a three-part treatment of angelic motion by asking whether angels move locally. Nine objections, chiefly from Aristotle's Physics, argue that an indivisible cannot traverse space, that motion arises from need, that angels lack potency and organs for natural or progressive motion, and that they would stay in their natural place. Albert, following Damascene and the saints, holds that angels do move locally, whatever the philosophers say. Aristotle's arguments apply to beings whose essence is indivisibility, such as the point and the unit. An angel's quantitative indivisibility merely follows from its being, and as a spiritual substance its power overcomes distance, time and resistance, so its motion is above nature. Angelic motion may manifest power or service rather than satisfy need. The power to move was given at creation, the will moves the angelic substance, and objections about natural motion do not apply.
claims: Aristotle's arguments against the motion of indivisibles do not apply to angels, whose indivisibility follows from their being rather than constituting it.
Angelic motion overcomes spatial distance and is not measured by time; it is above nature.
In the angel the will is mover and the substance moved, and motion need not arise from need.
